'''Thyrsa Anne Frazier Svager''' (June 16, 1930 – July 23, 1999) was an American academic who was the first African-American woman to earn a [[PhD]] in [[mathematics]] from [[Ohio State University]]. She was also the tenth African-American woman in the United States to earn this degree.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Hidden Figures Revealed |journal=Ohio State University Department of Mathematics |url=https://math.osu.edu/hidden-figures-revealed |access-date=16 March 2026}}</ref><ref name="Kenschaft">{{cite journal|last1=Kenschaft|first1=PD|author-link=Patricia Clark Kenschaft|title=Black women in mathematics in the United States|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|date=October 1981|volume=88|issue=8|pages=592–604|jstor=2320508|doi=10.1080/00029890.1981.11995321}}</ref> Born in Ohio, she graduated from high school at the age of 16, going to [[Antioch College]] in Ohio and then doing her postgraduate degrees at [[Ohio State University]].<ref name="NAM" /> Frazier Svager was the head of the Department of Mathematics at [[Central State University]] (CSU) in Ohio for decades, ending her academic career as provost and dean for academic affairs.<ref name="Parks" /> She and her husband, physics professor Aleksandar Svager, invested one of their salaries during their careers to build a legacy for scholarships.<ref name="APS News 2003">{{cite news|url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200302/svager.cfm|title=APS Member Gives Minority Scholarship Fund a Boost|date=February 2003|work=APS News|publisher=American Physical Society|volume= 12|issue=2|accessdate=April 16, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170506162704/https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200302/svager.cfm|archive-date=May 6, 2017}}</ref><ref name="YouTube" /> After her death, the Thyrsa Frazier Svager Fund was established to provide scholarships for African-American women majoring in mathematics.<ref name="Scholarship Fund" />

==Early life and education==

Frazier Svager was born Thyrsa Anne Frazier on June 16, 1930, in [[Wilberforce, Ohio]].<ref name="NAM">{{cite journal|last1=Houston|first1=Johnny L|title=Spotlight on a mathematician: Thyrsa Anne Frazier Svager 1930–1999|journal=National Association of Mathematics Newsletter|date=Summer 2000|volume=xxxi|issue=2|page=9|url=https://secure.portline.com/math/include/pages/files/newsletters/2000%20Summer.pdf|accessdate=April 18, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170419003218/https://secure.portline.com/math/include/pages/files/newsletters/2000%20Summer.pdf|archive-date=April 19, 2017|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}}</ref> Her mother, Elizabeth Anne Frazier, taught speech at [[Central State University]] (CSU), a historically black university in [[Wilberforce, Ohio]].<ref name="Parks" /> Her father, G. Thuton Frazier, headed the Logistics Department at the [[Wright-Patterson Air Force Base]] in [[Dayton, Ohio]].<ref name="Parks">{{cite book|last1=Parks|first1=Rena E. Lacey|title=All the White Folks: A History of a People|date=2010|publisher=Xlibris Corporation|location=Bloomington, IN|isbn=978-1465328090|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Xd6NAAAAQBAJ&pg=PT101|accessdate=April 16, 2017}}</ref> He was a member of the [[Kappa Alpha Psi]] fraternity, holding the position of Provence Polemarch.<ref name="Parks" /><ref name="Xenia DG – 2 July 1965">{{cite news|title=Receive key to city|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/39508589/|accessdate=April 16, 2017|work=Xenia Daily Gazette|date=July 2, 1965}}</ref> Frazier Svager had three sisters, Gail, Constance and Jane, and a brother, William Lafayette.<ref name="Parks" /><ref name="NAM" />

Frazier Svager graduated from Wilberforce University Preparatory Academy in Ohio at the age of 16 in 1947, as class [[valedictorian]].<ref name="NAM" /><ref name="Dayton Foundation bio" /> She attended [[Antioch College]], a private liberal arts college in [[Yellow Springs, Ohio]], majoring in mathematics, with a minor in chemistry, and placed in the 99th percentile in the Princeton Senior Student Examination.<ref name="XDG 10 Sept 1965">{{cite news|title=Miss Frazier receives PhD at Ohio State|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/39513791/|accessdate=April 16, 2017|work=Xenia Daily Gazette|date=September 10, 1965}}</ref> Frazier Svager was one of only four black students at Antioch: one of the others was [[Coretta Scott King]], with whom she was friends.<ref name="Dayton Foundation bio">{{cite web|title=Thyrsa Frazier Svager|url=https://daytonfoundation.academicworks.com/donors/thyrsa-frazier-svager|website=DaytonFoundation.AcademicWorks.com|publisher=The Dayton Foundation|accessdate=April 18, 2017}}</ref>

She gained a Bachelor of Arts degree from Antioch in 1951, going on to gain a master's (1952) and PhD from [[Ohio State University]] (OSU) in Columbus in 1965, where Paul Reichelderfer was her doctoral advisor.<ref name="MAA bio">{{cite web|last1=Kenschaft|first1=Patricia C|title=Thyrsa Anne Frazier Svager|url=http://www.maa.org/programs/underrepresented-groups/summa/summa-archival-record/thyrsa-frazier-svager|website=MAA.org|publisher=Mathematical Association of America|accessdate=April 16, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=10120}}</ref> Her dissertation was titled "On the product of absolutely continuous transformations of measure spaces".<ref name="Frazier Svager dissertation 1965">{{cite book|last1=Frazier|first1=Thyrsa Anne|title=On the product of absolutely continuous transformations of measure spaces|date=1965|publisher=Ohio State University|location=Columbus, OH|url=https://etd.ohiolink.edu/pg_10?0::NO:10:P10_ETD_SUBID:125877|accessdate=April 11, 2017}}</ref>

==Career==
Frazier Svager worked for a year at [[Wright-Patterson Air Force Base]] in Dayton, before teaching at [[Texas Southern University]] in [[Houston]].<ref name="MAA bio" /> In 1954, she joined the faculty of CSU in Wilberforce.<ref name="MAA bio" />

In 1967, Frazier Svager was appointed chairman of the department of mathematics.<ref name="XDG 12 June 1967">{{cite news|title=Several CSU department heads are changing|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/39499114/|accessdate=April 16, 2017|work=Xenia Daily Gazette|issue=June 12, 1967}}</ref> She was awarded tenure in 1970.<ref name="XDG July 1970">{{cite news|title=12 CSU faculty members promoted|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/42853956|accessdate=April 16, 2017|work=Xenia Daily Gazette|date=July 22, 1970}}</ref><ref name="MAA bio" /> She spent a summer in DC in 1966 as a systems analyst at [[NASA]], as visiting faculty at [[MIT]] in 1969, and in 1985, she undertook postdoctoral study at OSU during the summer.<ref name="NAM" /> She was provost and vice president for academic affairs when she retired in 1993.<ref name="Dayton Foundation bio" /><ref name="NAM" /> In March 1995, she returned for a short time to CSU as Interim President.<ref name="NAM" />

Frazier Svager was active on the issue of scholarships, serving as the president of the local chapter of MOLES, a national association that provided scholarships for college students.<ref name="XDG October 1971">{{cite news|title=MOLES chapter headed by Thyrsa Svager|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/39539503/|accessdate=April 16, 2017|work=Xenia Daily Gazette|date=October 6, 1971}}</ref> She was also a member of [[Beta Kappa Chi]], the [[National Association of Mathematicians]], and the [[Mathematical Association of America]], and was involved with [[Jack and Jill of America]].<ref name="XDG October 1971" /><ref name="NAM" /> Frazier Svager participated in the meeting that founded the National Association of Mathematics in 1969.<ref name="NAM" />

She wrote two books, CSU's ''Modern Elementary Algebra Workbook'' (1969),<ref name="OSU Algebra Workbook">{{cite book|last1=Central State University, Department of Mathematics|title=Modern elementary algebra workbook|year=1972|publisher=W.C. Brown Book Co|location=Dubuque|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mSwhAQAAIAAJ&pg=PA829|accessdate=April 18, 2017}}</ref> and ''Essential Mathematics for College Freshmen'' (1976).<ref name="CSU Freshmen">{{cite book|last1=Central State University, Department of Mathematics|title=Essential mathematics for College freshmen|date=August 25, 1976|publisher=Kendall Hunt|location=Ohio|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_kshAQAAIAAJ&pg=PA2646|accessdate=April 18, 2017}}</ref>

==Personal life==
While on the CSU faculty, Frazier met Aleksandar Svager, a Holocaust survivor from Yugoslavia and physics professor at CSU.<ref name="APS News 2003" /><ref name="YouTube" /> They married in June 1968 at her parents' home.<ref name="XDG 19 June 1968">{{cite news|title=Marriage solemnized Sunday|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/42848446/|accessdate=April 16, 2017|work=Xenia Daily Gazette|date=June 19, 1968}}</ref>

Thyrsa Frazier Svager died on July 23, 1999.<ref name="Buffalo">{{cite web|title=Black women in mathematics: Thyrsa Frazier Svager|url=http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/PEEPS/svager_thyrsa_f.html|website=Math.Buffalo.Edu|publisher=Buffalo University|accessdate=April 18, 2017}}</ref>

==Philanthropy==
Both university professors with a strong commitment to furthering education opportunities, the Svagers lived on one income, investing the other to build a scholarship fund.<ref name="YouTube">{{cite web|title=Thrysa Frazier Svager: One of Dayton's Hidden Figures|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6TTR_7cyqFQ|website=YouTube| date=February 16, 2017 |publisher=The Dayton Foundation|accessdate=April 18, 2017}}</ref> After her death, her husband established the Thyrsa Frazier Svager Fund at the Dayton Foundation, for African-American women who major in mathematics at one of six universities, with a legacy contribution planned.<ref name="Scholarship Fund">{{cite web|title=Thyrsa Frazier Svager Scholarship Fund|url=https://daytonfoundation.academicworks.com/opportunities/4016|website=DaytonFoundation.AcademicWorks.com|publisher=The Dayton Foundation|accessdate=April 18, 2017}}</ref><ref name="YouTube" /> As of February 2017, 33 women had received support from the Fund.<ref name="YouTube" /> An annual contribution is also being made to the [[American Physical Society]]'s Minority Scholarship.<ref name="APS News 2003" /> Alongside her professional career, Thyrsa was active as a member of various civil and social organizations. She was a member of, among others, [[Alpha Kappa Alpha]] sorority, Twentieth Century Club, Wilberforce Chapter of Moles, and Volunteers of the African American Museum.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Alpha |first=Alpha Kappa |date=1992 |title=Ivies Beyond the Wall |journal=Ivy Leaf |volume=69 |issue=4 |pages=71 |via=LexisNexis}}</ref>

==Honors==
Frazier Svager was honored with an Honorary [[Doctor of Humane Letters]] by CSU on her retirement, and she was inducted into the Hall of Fame in [[Greene County, Ohio]].<ref name="NAM" />
